# TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC, Reno and BBR

TCP will send as much as the *path* will hold, not as much as the application can write. The congestion-control algorithm is the part of the stack that decides how large that in-flight window is allowed to be, and how it reacts when the path seems busy. On Linux the default has been **CUBIC** for many years. **Reno** (and its NewReno repair) is the historical loss-based baseline. **BBR** (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time) is a model-based alternative that estimates the bottleneck rate and the minimum RTT instead of treating every lost packet as a signal to cut the window in half. This chapter shows how to *see* which algorithm a socket is using, how to select one per socket, and what CUBIC and BBR actually optimise — including the cases where a popular “just enable BBR” tip is wrong.

## Learning goals

- Read `net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control`, `tcp_available_congestion_control` and `tcp_allowed_congestion_control`, and pick an algorithm with `TCP_CONGESTION`
- Read the algorithm name, `cwnd`, `rtt`, `pmtu`, and `app_limited` from `ss -ti`, and know which numbers you must not quote as a benchmark
- Explain CUBIC’s loss-based cubic growth (RFC 8312 / RFC 9438) versus Reno’s linear growth after a multiplicative decrease
- Explain what BBRv1 estimated, why BBRv2/v3 exist, and when BBR can be harder on a loss-based neighbor
- Say what this kernel can and cannot load (no BBR module here)

**Version note.** Sysctls and labs ran on 2026-11-13 on Linux **6.12.94+** with iproute2 **6.15.0** and Python 3.13.5. The host reports `tcp_available_congestion_control = reno cubic` and the default `tcp_congestion_control = cubic`. There is no loadable `tcp_bbr` module in `/lib/modules` on this writing host. `setsockopt(TCP_CONGESTION, "bbr")` and a sysctl write of `bbr` both failed with `No such file or directory`. CUBIC and Reno transfers ran in two `unshare` network namespaces connected by a veth (`192.0.2.1` → `192.0.2.2`, MTU 1500). `ss -ti` listings below are pasted from those runs. There is no `tc` / netem on this host, so the path has essentially no delay and no induced loss: the transfer finishes in a few milliseconds and the implied `send` rates are arithmetic, not capacity measurements. BBR behaviour is written from the kernel’s TCP BBR documentation and the IETF work, and is **not run** here.

The transport chapter covers TCP and UDP generally. A sibling chapter already uses `ss -ti` as a troubleshooting tool; this one is about the congestion-control name on that line.

## The knobs Linux actually exposes

Three sysctls, all under `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/`:

| Sysctl | This host | Role |
|--------|-----------|------|
| `tcp_available_congestion_control` | `reno cubic` | Algorithms compiled in or already loaded |
| `tcp_allowed_congestion_control` | `reno cubic` | Algorithms a non-privileged socket may choose |
| `tcp_congestion_control` | `cubic` | Default for new sockets |

On this host they were:

```text
# uname -r
6.12.94+
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_available_congestion_control
reno cubic
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_allowed_congestion_control
reno cubic
# cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_congestion_control
cubic
```

`reno` is built into the core TCP code. CUBIC is a module that this kernel has already loaded (or compiled in). BBR is a different module (`tcp_bbr`). If it is not in `available`, you cannot select it:

```text
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='cubic' -> getsockopt='cubic' OK
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='reno' -> getsockopt='reno' OK
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr2' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='bbr3' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
setsockopt TCP_CONGESTION='yeah' -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
write tcp_congestion_control=bbr -> [Errno 2] No such file or directory
value still: cubic
```

That `ENOENT` is the kernel telling you the algorithm is not present, not that you lacked capability. Loading `tcp_bbr` would take a privileged `modprobe` (and a module that exists). This host has neither; nothing was loaded. Do not assume “modern Linux means BBR is there.” Check `available` first.

A process chooses an algorithm for one socket with `setsockopt` level `IPPROTO_TCP`, option `TCP_CONGESTION` (value 13), passing the name as a string. Unprivileged processes may only pick names in `tcp_allowed_congestion_control`. Changing the *default* sysctl is a system-wide (or netns-wide) act and is usually the wrong first move; prefer a per-service setsockopt or a `systemd` / `ip-tcp_metrics` policy you can roll back.

## Reading `ss -ti` without lying to yourself

The algorithm name is the first token on the indented `ss -ti` line. Next to it sit `cwnd` (congestion window, in *segments*), `rtt` (smoothed RTT / variance, in milliseconds), `pmtu`, `mss`, and often `app_limited` or a huge `send` figure.

An 8 MiB write from `192.0.2.1` to `192.0.2.2` across a veth, mid-transfer, CUBIC on the sending socket:

```text
# ss -ti mid-transfer cubic client 192.0.2.1 -> 192.0.2.2:45111
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          192.0.2.1:53180    192.0.2.2:45111
	 cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.049/0.058 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:536 advmss:1448 cwnd:897 bytes_sent:2162688 bytes_acked:2162689 segs_out:1506 segs_in:30 data_segs_out:1504 send 212Gbps lastsnd:4 lastrcv:4 lastack:4 pacing_rate 424Gbps delivery_rate 5.79Gbps delivered:1505 rcv_space:14480 rcv_ssthresh:64088 minrtt:0.002 snd_wnd:4138624 rcv_wnd:64256
```

The same transfer with the sending socket set to Reno:

```text
# ss -ti mid-transfer reno client 192.0.2.1 -> 192.0.2.2:45112
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB 0      0          192.0.2.1:34960    192.0.2.2:45112
	 reno wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:0.044/0.035 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:536 advmss:1448 cwnd:994 bytes_sent:2162688 bytes_acked:2162689 segs_out:1501 segs_in:20 data_segs_out:1499 send 262Gbps pacing_rate 516Gbps delivery_rate 644Mbps delivered:1500 rcv_space:14480 rcv_ssthresh:64088 minrtt:0.003 snd_wnd:1575808 rcv_wnd:64256
```

Both sides received the full 8 MiB (`recvd=8388608`) in about 5–6 ms. What to trust:

- The **name** (`cubic` / `reno`) is the algorithm on *that* socket. The listening side, if you snapshot it, may still say `cubic` because the server never called `setsockopt`. Congestion control is a sender decision.
- **`pmtu:1500`** and **`mss:1448`** show this is a real Ethernet-sized path (1500 minus headers), not the loopback `pmtu:65535` / 32 KiB MSS you will see on `127.0.0.1`.
- **`cwnd:897`** and **`cwnd:994`** are huge because the path has no delay and no loss. The window opened as fast as ACKs returned. On a 30 ms, slightly lossy WAN path you would see a much smaller `cwnd` and a meaningful difference between the algorithms.
- **`send 212Gbps`** is `cwnd * mss / rtt` with an RTT of 49 *microseconds*. It is not a measurement of the NIC, the veth, or CUBIC. Do not publish it. `delivery_rate` is a little closer to observed throughput, and even that is a nearly idle or already-finished burst on this path.
- The transfer time (`0.0060s` / `0.0045s`) is also not a CUBIC-versus-Reno result. Without queueing delay or loss, both algorithms just get out of the way.

If you need a fair comparison, you want a path with a known bandwidth-delay product and a controlled loss or queue (for example `netem` on a lab host that has `tc`). That lab was not run here.

## Loss-based control: Reno and CUBIC

Classic TCP, as popularised by Reno / NewReno, treats a lost segment (or a sufficient ECN mark, when ECN is in use) as congestion. The window is cut — multiplicatively, typically to about half for a fast retransmit — and then grows linearly, one more segment per RTT in congestion avoidance. On a high-bandwidth, high-RTT path that linear climb is slow: after a single loss it can take many RTTs to fill the pipe again.

**CUBIC** (RFC 8312, later RFC 9438) stays loss-based, but the window is a cubic function of *time since the last congestion event*, not of ACK count. After a cut, CUBIC grows slowly around the previous operating point (to probe whether the path is still full), then more quickly if that point is left behind, and it flattens again as it approaches the old window. Time-based growth is why CUBIC is less punished by a long RTT than Reno is, and why it became the Linux default.

CUBIC still *believes* loss is congestion. On a path with random wireless loss, or a shallow switch queue that drops while the path is not actually full, both Reno and CUBIC back off. That is the design. It is also the complaint that motivated BBR.

## Model-based control: BBR

BBR, originally from Cardwell et al. at Google and documented in the Linux kernel’s `tcp_bbr` notes and subsequent IETF drafts, estimates two numbers: the bottleneck bandwidth (from delivered rate over time) and the round-trip *propagation* delay (from the minimum RTT seen). The product is the bandwidth-delay product, the amount of data that should be in flight to fill the pipe but not the queue. BBR paces at the estimated rate and caps in-flight data around that product, with periodic probes for more bandwidth and for a new minimum RTT.

The intended contrast with CUBIC is simple:

| | CUBIC / Reno | BBR |
|---|---|---|
| Primary signal | Loss (and ECN, if enabled) | Estimated rate and min RTT |
| Reaction to random loss | Shrink `cwnd` | Should keep the rate if the model still says the pipe is not full |
| Risk | Underfills a long-fat path after loss | Can fill a *shared* queue more aggressively than a loss-based neighbor, and early BBRv1 was known to do so |

BBRv1’s queueing behaviour on paths it shared with CUBIC was the reason for **BBRv2** and later **BBRv3**: more conservative reaction to loss and ECN, better coexistence. Linux module and `ss` names vary by tree (`bbr`, sometimes a versioned name). This host has none of them, so there is no `ss -ti` line to paste.

Two operational consequences matter more than the brand name:

1. **You cannot enable BBR if it is not in `available`.** The `ENOENT` above is the whole story until the module exists and is allowed.
2. **Switching a whole server to BBR because a blog said “three sysctls make it faster” is not a measurement.** BBR can help a long, slightly lossy path where CUBIC keeps backing off; it can also change how your flows share a bottleneck with CUBIC-only peers. Measure with `ss -ti` and an application-level goodput on a representative path, and keep a way to revert the default.

## Choosing one, in practice

- Leave the system default at CUBIC unless you have a reason and a rollback.
- If a single service needs a different algorithm, set `TCP_CONGESTION` in that process (or its unit / container) after checking `tcp_allowed_congestion_control`.
- Compare algorithms on a path that looks like production (delay, modest loss, a real MTU), not on a veth with a 50 µs RTT.
- Watch `app_limited`. If the application is not offering enough data, the algorithm is not the bottleneck and `cwnd` / `send` will mislead you.

## Gotchas

- **Quoting `send …Gbps` from a lab with a tiny RTT.** The formula will invent a fantasy rate. Look at elapsed time, `delivery_rate`, and application counters instead.
- **Assuming both ends of `ss -ti` show the algorithm you set.** Only the sending socket’s choice matters for that direction; the listener may still say `cubic`.
- **Loopback or same-namespace local delivery.** `pmtu:65535` means you are not on a 1500-byte path. The veth lab above was set up in two netns precisely so `pmtu:1500` would show up.
- **“The kernel is 6.12, so BBR is there.”** Availability is a module/config question, not a version number. Read `tcp_available_congestion_control`.
- **No netem, no comparison.** Without delay or loss, CUBIC and Reno mid-transfer windows in this lab were both enormous (`cwnd` 897 vs 994) and the elapsed times were within a couple of milliseconds. That is not a result.

## Boring rule

Read the algorithm name and `cwnd` from `ss -ti`, but only trust a comparison when the path has a real RTT and a reason to lose or queue packets. Check `available` before you try to “turn on BBR.”

## Try this

1. On a lab host that has `tc`, add 20–50 ms and a fraction of a percent of loss on a veth, repeat the 8 MiB transfer with CUBIC and Reno, and compare elapsed time and mid-transfer `cwnd`. Then, if `bbr` is in `available`, add it as a third run.
2. Set `TCP_CONGESTION` to `reno` on only the client and confirm the server’s `ss -ti` line still says `cubic`.
3. Start a transfer, pause the sender so the socket goes `app_limited`, and watch `send` and `cwnd` stop meaning “path capacity.”

- RFC 8312, *CUBIC for Fast Long-Distance Networks*; RFC 9438, *CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks* (standards-track update)
- RFC 5681, *TCP Congestion Control* (Reno-style loss-based control)
- Linux kernel documentation for `tcp_congestion_control` / BBR (`Documentation/networking/bbr-quick-start` and the `tcp_bbr` module notes in the tree you run)
- `ss(8)`, iproute2 6.15; `tcp(7)` (`TCP_CONGESTION`)
- Cardwell, Cheng, Gunn, Yeganeh, Jacobson, *BBR: Congestion-Based Congestion Control* (the original description); later IETF CCWG work on BBRv2/v3 for coexistence
